meta.label: Email
meta.attribution: Built from providers' own encryption and privacy documentation, source repositories where published, pricing pages, and, where cited, Ethical Consumer's independent email guide and regulator records, not measured data. Email policies and defaults change, so check the current documentation yourself before relying on any of these. Privacy reflects whether the provider can read the contents of an ordinary email, not just whether the connection is encrypted in transit; openness reflects whether client or server code is published and under what licence; portability reflects whether a mailbox uses IMAP or another standard protocol that lets a person move to another provider or client without losing mail; respect reflects whether the business model runs on advertising or reading message content rather than a subscription or donations; accessibility covers how easy a mailbox is to set up and use, including with ordinary mail apps. Compared here are mailbox services a person sends and receives mail from. Alias and forwarding services (SimpleLogin, addy.io, Firefox Relay, DuckDuckGo Email Protection, Hide My Email), separate mail client apps (Thunderbird, K-9 Mail, FairEmail), Delta Chat, and mailbox reputation or blacklist checkers do a different job and are not compared here. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare email by privacy, everyday access, openness, and data portability.

criteria.label: Encrypted, not read by the provider
Easy to set up and use with ordinary mail apps

products.name: Proton Mail

privacy.note: Proton says zero-access encryption means it never sees the inbox on any plan, and that not even Proton can read a user's emails.

openness.note: Proton publishes open-source client and security-audit material for its apps on GitHub, though the mail server stack itself is not published.

portability.note: Proton documents import and export tools for moving mail in and out of an account, though moving between encrypted-mail providers has more friction than ordinary IMAP mail.

respect.note: Proton says it does not sell ads and funds itself through paid privacy services rather than advertising.

accessibility.note: Proton Mail has web and mobile apps and a free tier, though its encrypted workflow is a different pattern from plain webmail.

economical.note: The free plan gives 1 GB of storage and one address; paid Mail Plus and Proton Unlimited plans add storage, more addresses and custom domains.

products.description: An encrypted mailbox that says it cannot read a user's email on any plan, with open-source clients and a permanent free tier alongside paid storage upgrades.

products.name: Tuta

privacy.note: Tuta says it end-to-end encrypts emails including subject lines and attachments, entire calendars including event metadata, and the full address book; sender and recipient addresses stay unencrypted because the email protocol requires them.

openness.note: Tuta publishes its app source code publicly on GitHub.

portability.note: Because Tuta encrypts subject lines and does not use standard IMAP, mail cannot be read through an ordinary external mail client the way unencrypted IMAP mail can.

respect.note: Tuta presents itself as ad-free privacy software funded by paying users rather than advertising.

accessibility.note: The free Basic plan includes 1 GB of storage, one calendar and encryption by default, but the encrypted-by-default design is a different workflow from ordinary webmail.

economical.note: The Basic plan is free; paid Revolutionary and Legend plans add storage, custom domains and calendar sharing, with extra family members priced separately.

products.description: A German encrypted mailbox that end-to-end encrypts subject lines and attachments as well as message bodies, with open-source clients and a permanent free tier.

products.name: Fastmail

privacy.note: Fastmail's privacy policy does not describe end-to-end encryption; it says data is protected with SSL/TLS encryption during transmission, and that IP logs are kept for up to a year to monitor for fraud.

openness.note: Fastmail supports open mail standards including IMAP, SMTP, CardDAV and CalDAV, though the hosted service itself is proprietary.

portability.note: Standard-protocol support and documented export tools make it straightforward to use Fastmail with an external mail client or move data elsewhere.

respect.note: Fastmail's privacy policy says it does not sell personal information and has never trained AI on customer data.

accessibility.note: Fastmail's apps and standard-client compatibility are polished, but there is no permanent free tier, only a 30-day free trial.

economical.note: Individual plans start at 6 US dollars a month with 60 GB of storage after a 30-day free trial; there is no free consumer tier.

products.description: A paid, standards-friendly mailbox that supports ordinary IMAP clients and says it does not sell data, but is not end-to-end encrypted and has no permanent free tier.

products.name: Gmail

privacy.note: Google's privacy policy says it does not show personalized ads based on content from Gmail, Drive or Photos, though Gmail content is still processed as part of a broader Google account.

openness.note: Gmail is a closed Google service; there is no published client or server source, though it supports standard mail protocols in third-party apps.

portability.note: Google Takeout lets a user export Gmail messages, preserving labels in a special header in the downloaded file.

respect.note: Google says it does not personalize ads from Gmail content, but Gmail sits inside the same account used for search, YouTube and location data that do feed ad personalization elsewhere.

accessibility.note: Gmail is free, with a polished web and mobile interface, spam filtering and broad third-party integration.

economical.note: Consumer Gmail is free, with paid storage and Google Workspace upgrades.

products.description: The dominant free mailbox: an easy, familiar interface and portable export tools, but built inside Google's wider advertising and account ecosystem.

products.name: Outlook.com Mail

privacy.note: Microsoft's privacy statement says a person can download their Outlook.com email through their privacy settings, and that Microsoft does not use email content to target ads.

openness.note: Outlook.com is a proprietary Microsoft service, though Outlook apps can connect to standard mail accounts.

portability.note: Exporting an Outlook.com mailbox to a .pst file requires installing desktop Outlook rather than a simple web download; Mac users need legacy Outlook for Mac and an .olm file.

respect.note: Microsoft's privacy statement says it does not use what a person writes in email to target ads, but the free tier of Outlook.com still shows inbox ads unless a person pays for Microsoft 365.

accessibility.note: A mature web and mobile app, a widely held Microsoft account, and Office integration make Outlook.com easy for many people to adopt.

economical.note: The basic mailbox is free; ad-free use, more storage and advanced security need a paid Microsoft 365 plan.

products.description: A highly accessible mainstream mailbox with strong Microsoft integration, but closed, ad-supported on free accounts, and exportable only through desktop Outlook software.

products.name: Yahoo Mail

privacy.note: Yahoo's privacy policy says it analyzes email content, specifically emails from retailers and other organizations rather than personal emails between individuals, to build advertising interest profiles, and that people can opt out through privacy settings.

openness.note: Yahoo Mail is a proprietary hosted email service.

portability.note: Yahoo documents downloading mailbox content through IMAP into third-party email apps.

respect.note: The SEC found in 2018 that Yahoo, by then renamed Altaba, concealed from investors for more than two years a 2014 breach in which hackers stole usernames, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, encrypted passwords and security questions for hundreds of millions of accounts, and it paid a 35 million dollar penalty.

accessibility.note: Yahoo Mail is free, web-based and broadly available, though less central to most people's daily workflow than Gmail or Outlook.

economical.note: Yahoo Mail is free, with paid upgrades for more features and fewer ads.

products.description: A free, familiar mailbox that is a useful floor for comparison: its own privacy policy describes analyzing commercial email to build ad-interest profiles, and the SEC found its operator concealed a massive breach from investors for two years.

products.name: iCloud Mail

privacy.note: Apple's security overview says iCloud Mail does not use end-to-end encryption because of the need to interoperate with the global email system, and that Apple holds the keys.

openness.note: iCloud Mail is a proprietary Apple service; Apple's own guide says a person must sign in with an Apple Account to create or use an iCloud Mail address.

portability.note: Apple Mail can export mailboxes as .mbox packages, and iCloud Mail also works through standard mail clients.

respect.note: iCloud Mail carries no ads and is bundled with a free Apple ID, though it is built to keep a person inside Apple devices and paid iCloud storage rather than as an independent product.

accessibility.note: For Apple users, Mail is built into every device and available at iCloud.com; it is less useful for anyone using other platforms day to day.

economical.note: The mailbox is included with a free Apple ID, though heavy use requires paid iCloud storage.

products.description: A bundled, ad-free Apple mailbox with decent standards support, but Apple's own security overview says it is not end-to-end encrypted and that Apple holds the keys.

products.name: Zoho Mail

privacy.note: Zoho says it does not sell data to third parties and restricts employee access to customer data to a small, monitored group.

openness.note: Zoho Mail is a proprietary hosted service, though it supports conventional mail administration and client workflows.

portability.note: Zoho documents ZIP and PST export options for administrators and per-folder export for users.

respect.note: Zoho says no ads are displayed in Zoho Mail and that it will never sell user data, which is a paid-business rather than advertising model.

accessibility.note: The free Forever plan covers up to five users with 5 GB of storage each and one custom domain, aimed more at small organizations than casual personal email.

economical.note: Zoho Mail has a permanent free plan for up to five users, with low-cost paid Mail Lite and Mail Premium tiers for more storage.

products.description: A business-friendly ad-free mailbox with a permanent free tier and a stated no-data-sale policy, but proprietary and aimed more at small organizations than casual personal email.

products.name: Mailbox.org

privacy.note: Mailbox.org advertises ad-free, GDPR-compliant email protected with Transport Layer Security for all messages, with optional PGP or S/MIME end-to-end encryption in its webmail client.

openness.note: The hosted service is proprietary, but supports open protocols including IMAP, POP3 and SMTP.

portability.note: Mailbox.org offers a data-export feature covering email, calendars, contacts, files and tasks in open formats.

respect.note: Mailbox.org markets itself as no advertising, no tracking and hosted in Germany; it was spun out of its parent Heinlein Support GmbH into the separate company Heinlein Hosting GmbH in 2021.

accessibility.note: It offers webmail and standard-client support, but is less polished for casual users than the big free providers, and there is no permanent free plan, only a 30-day trial.

economical.note: Private plans start at 1 euro a month for the Light tier, after a 30-day free trial.

products.description: A strong paid privacy mailbox: ad-free, standards-friendly and export-conscious, hosted in Germany, but with no permanent free tier and less beginner hand-holding than the biggest free providers.

products.name: Posteo

privacy.note: Posteo says signup needs no personal information, its website does not save IP addresses or use tracking tools, and it supports S/MIME or OpenPGP encryption.

openness.note: Posteo is not a fully open-source hosted service, but supports open protocols including IMAP, POP3, CalDAV, CardDAV, PGP and S/MIME.

portability.note: Standard-protocol support lets a person use Posteo through an external mail client, though it is not a one-click export product.

respect.note: Posteo has no permanent free plan; every account is paid from the start, at 1 euro a month, funding an ad-free, tracking-free design rather than an advertising or freemium model.

accessibility.note: It offers webmail and client support, but there is no free account at all, and the anonymous signup and encryption options are less familiar than mainstream webmail.

economical.note: A Posteo account costs 1 euro a month, with small add-ons for more storage, extra aliases and calendars.

products.description: A lean privacy mailbox with anonymous signup and no free tier at all: every account is paid from day one, at 1 euro a month, which is what funds its no-tracking design.

products.name: StartMail

privacy.note: StartMail says privacy was its objective from the start, and it encrypts stored email and blocks remote content by default.

openness.note: StartMail is a proprietary hosted email service rather than an open-source mailbox platform.

portability.note: StartMail supports IMAP access through a trusted-device password, so external mail clients and migration are practical.

respect.note: StartMail is operated by StartMail B.V. in Zeist, the Netherlands, and is a paid privacy product with aliases and encryption rather than an advertising-funded free mailbox.

accessibility.note: It works through webmail and standard clients, but there is only a short free trial and a smaller support ecosystem than mainstream mail.

economical.note: StartMail offers a short free trial; ongoing personal use is billed monthly or annually.

products.description: A paid Dutch privacy mailbox with aliases and IMAP support, useful for escaping ad-funded mail, but with only a short free trial and a smaller ecosystem than mainstream providers.

products.name: Mailfence

privacy.note: Mailfence says it offers browser-based end-to-end encrypted email with no ads or trackers.

openness.note: Mailfence is operated by ContactOffice Group sa, a Belgian company registered in Brussels, and uses interoperable mail standards, but the hosted platform itself is not published as open source.

portability.note: Mailfence documents backup and export tools and recommends IMAP clients for large backups, though full email backup is not available on the free tier.

respect.note: Mailfence says it has no ads, trackers or targeted-ad data commercialization, and runs on infrastructure it controls in Belgium rather than a foreign parent's cloud.

accessibility.note: It offers a free entry tier and a full email suite, but PGP-based encrypted workflows are less familiar than mainstream webmail.

economical.note: A free tier gives 500 MB of email storage; paid tiers add more storage, aliases and backup capability.

products.description: A Belgian privacy-mail suite operated by ContactOffice Group, with a free entry tier, a no-ad stance and PGP-based encryption, balanced by proprietary hosting and export limits on the free tier.

products.name: HEY

privacy.note: HEY's FAQ says the email database is encrypted at rest, but that 'HEY is not end-to-end encrypted (we still hold the keys)'; staff decryption is logged and reviewed weekly by a separate team.

openness.note: HEY only works through its own web, Mac, Windows, iOS and Android apps; its FAQ says off-the-shelf third-party email apps won't work with it, and HEY's pages describe no published source code.

portability.note: HEY's FAQ says 'HEY doesn't support IMAP or POP' and does not import old mail, but a user can export all mail as an MBOX file and contacts as a vCard at any time, and paid users can forward their address elsewhere forever.

respect.note: The 37signals privacy policy, updated September 2026, says 'We never sell your data', that no human looks at content except with express permission, and that its products do not use customer content to train AI models.

accessibility.note: HEY has polished apps on every major platform and a 30-day trial with no card required, but no free plan, no IMAP for ordinary mail apps, and a deliberately different screen-first workflow.

economical.note: HEY for You costs 99 US dollars a year, billed annually only; HEY for Domains is 12 dollars per user a month, and a family plan for up to five people is 179 dollars a year.

products.description: A paid, ad-free mailbox from the makers of Basecamp that screens first-time senders, but holds the encryption keys, works only in its own apps with no IMAP, and has no free tier.

products.name: GMX Mail

privacy.note: GMX's privacy policy says inventory and content data are used for analyses to optimize products if a user has given consent, and points users to settings for interest-based advertising; mail is not end-to-end encrypted unless a user opts in to PGP.

openness.note: GMX is a proprietary hosted service run by 1&1 Mail & Media GmbH; its optional encryption uses the open OpenPGP standard through the Mailvelope browser extension.

portability.note: GMX's help centre publishes IMAP and SMTP server settings (imap.gmx.com, port 993) for syncing a GMX mailbox with third-party mail programs such as Thunderbird, Outlook and Apple Mail.

respect.note: GMX's privacy policy describes interest-based online advertising on the free service, which users have to revoke through its permission settings.

accessibility.note: GMX offers a free account with 65 GB of email storage, up to 10 alias addresses, 50 MB attachments and mobile apps for Android and iOS.

economical.note: The basic GMX mailbox is free, with 65 GB of email storage.

products.description: A large free German-run mailbox with generous storage and standard IMAP access, funded by advertising, with optional PGP encryption through a browser extension rather than by default.

products.name: AOL Mail

privacy.note: AOL's privacy policy, updated September 2026, lists 'the content of incoming and outgoing emails and attachments' among the data it processes for smart email features such as automatically identifying travel bookings, on the basis of consent or legitimate interest depending on jurisdiction.

openness.note: AOL Mail is a proprietary hosted service from AOL Media LLC; Bending Spoons lists AOL among the companies it acquired, in January 2026.

portability.note: AOL Help publishes a guide to using POP or IMAP to sync AOL Mail on a third-party app or download a copy of a mailbox.

respect.note: AOL's privacy policy says it processes data to show personalized advertising, including by installing third-party tracking technologies, and shares data with advertising networks.

accessibility.note: AOL Mail is free, with web access, an iOS and Android app, support in over 70 languages and phone experts available around the clock.

economical.note: AOL says it is quick and easy to sign up for a free AOL account that includes AOL Mail.

products.description: A long-running free mailbox, now owned by Bending Spoons, that supports IMAP but whose privacy policy covers processing email content for smart features and tracking-based personalized advertising.

products.name: Infomaniak Mail

privacy.note: Infomaniak's guide says optional encryption, switched on per message, encrypts mail and attachments on its servers with OpenPGP keys that are stored in Infomaniak's data centres and unlocked automatically by Infomaniak login, so it is not zero-access; mail not sent this way is not covered.

openness.note: Infomaniak publishes its Android Mail app on GitHub under the GPL-3.0 licence; the hosted mail service itself is not published.

portability.note: Infomaniak's guide gives standard IMAP (mail.infomaniak.com, port 993) and SMTP settings and set-up guides for Outlook, Apple Mail, Thunderbird, Gmail and Android mail apps, using a generated per-device password.

respect.note: Infomaniak lists 'No advertising' among the features of my kSuite and says it does not finance its free services by selling personal data; services are developed and hosted in Switzerland.

accessibility.note: The free my kSuite plan gives one @ik.me, @etik.com or @ikmail.com address with 20 GB of mail storage, web and mobile apps and a set-up wizard for common mail apps, though signup needs a phone number from a listed country.

economical.note: my kSuite is free for life with 20 GB of mail storage and 15 GB of cloud storage; the paid tier with unlimited mail storage starts at 1.60 Swiss francs a month.

products.description: A Swiss ad-free mailbox with a generous free tier, standard IMAP and open-source mobile apps, whose optional encryption keeps keys on Infomaniak's own servers rather than with the user.

products.name: Disroot

privacy.note: Disroot's privacy policy says all emails, unless encrypted by the user with GnuPG/PGP, are stored unencrypted on its servers, which use full disk encryption, and that it does not analyse behaviour to build profiles.

openness.note: Disroot says it uses '100% free and open source software', meaning its source code is publicly accessible and can be audited.

portability.note: Disroot publishes IMAP, POP and SMTP settings and suggests clients including Thunderbird, K-9 Mail, FairEmail and the iOS Mail app.

respect.note: Disroot's privacy policy says it has 'no advertisements or business relationships with advertisers' and does not sell data; the project is run by volunteers in Amsterdam and relies on community donations.

accessibility.note: Accounts work through Roundcube webmail or any desktop or mobile client, but the mailbox is capped at 1 GB and the service is run by a small volunteer team.

economical.note: The 1 GB mailbox is free; extra storage is paid, and a custom domain is offered as a perk for donors.

products.description: A volunteer-run, donation-funded Dutch mailbox built entirely on free software, with standard IMAP and no advertising, but a 1 GB limit and mail stored unencrypted unless users add PGP.

products.name: Runbox

privacy.note: Ethical Consumer's February 2025 email guide placed Runbox in its 70 to 80 out of 100 band for privacy, with a highest-privacy jurisdiction and essential-only data sharing, but did not list it among providers with end-to-end encryption as standard.

openness.note: Runbox publishes its Runbox 7 webmail on GitHub under GPLv3 or later, but the README says the full Runbox backend 'is not yet open source'.

portability.note: Runbox supports access through the web, POP, IMAP and SMTP, with CardDAV contacts and CalDAV calendars.

respect.note: Runbox's privacy policy says 'We do not use any advertisements', that it does not scan email to display ads, uses no third-party tracking, and will not sell user data.

accessibility.note: Every plan has a 30-day free trial with no card required and a 60-day money-back guarantee, but there is no permanent free plan.

economical.note: The smallest Micro plan is 19.95 euros a year for 2 GB of mail; the Mini plan is 34.95 euros a year for 10 GB, with cheaper subaccounts for family members.

products.description: A paid Norwegian mailbox running on hydropower, with full IMAP and DAV support, an open-source webmail and a no-ads, no-scanning policy, but no permanent free plan.

products.name: Kolab Now

privacy.note: Ethical Consumer's February 2025 email guide gave Kolab Now 100 out of 100 for privacy and listed it among providers with a highest-privacy jurisdiction and essential-only data sharing.

openness.note: Kolab Now says there are 'No proprietary components on our systems. Everything we do is Open Source (FOSS) and open standards'.

portability.note: Kolab Now publishes standard IMAP (imap.kolabnow.com, port 993) and SMTP settings for any generic client, and says open standards mean users are not affected by vendor lock-in.

respect.note: Kolab Now says no data broker gets access to user data, that data is not sold, and that it takes no venture capital investment; it is paid for by subscriptions.

accessibility.note: Any standard desktop or mobile client can connect, and new customers get a free four-week trial, but there is no permanent free plan.

economical.note: Kolab Now's pricing page lists the Just Email plan at 5.00 Swiss francs a month with 5 GB of storage, and Full Kolab with calendar, files and document editing at 9.90 francs a month; the first 30 days are free.

products.description: A Swiss paid mail and groupware service built entirely on open-source software and open standards, rated top for privacy by Ethical Consumer, but with no free tier and relatively high per-user prices.

products.name: Hushmail

privacy.note: Hushmail's privacy policy says encrypted email is stored encrypted but unencrypted email is stored unencrypted, and it logs sender and recipient addresses and subjects.

openness.note: Hushmail uses the open OpenPGP standard for encryption, but it is a proprietary hosted service and its pages describe no published source code for the current service.

portability.note: The Personal plan can be used with Apple Mail or Microsoft Outlook over POP or IMAP, as well as on the web and an iPhone app.

respect.note: Hushmail's privacy policy says 'We do not analyze the email in your account for the purpose of displaying advertisements' and will never sell personal information, though it may share non-identifying data to support its own marketing.

accessibility.note: Hushmail now mainly targets healthcare and legal practices; the Personal plan offers one-click OpenPGP encryption and support by chat, email and phone, but no free tier and no custom domains.

economical.note: Hushmail for Personal Use costs 59.99 US dollars a year, with a 60-day money-back guarantee and no free plan.

products.description: A veteran Canadian encrypted-email service, now aimed mainly at healthcare practices, with a paid personal plan and IMAP access, but plain mail stored unencrypted and a record of handing decrypted mail to authorities under court order.

products.name: GreenNet

privacy.note: Ethical Consumer's February 2025 email guide listed GreenNet among providers offering end-to-end encryption as standard, with essential-only data sharing, and placed it in its 70 to 80 out of 100 privacy band.

openness.note: GreenNet's webmail runs on Roundcube, an open-source webmail project, though Ethical Consumer did not list GreenNet among providers with open-source code.

portability.note: The Just Email plan includes IMAP, POP and SMTP access alongside Roundcube webmail.

respect.note: Ethical Consumer describes GreenNet as not-for-profit and scored it 88 out of 100 overall, the highest in its email guide.

accessibility.note: GreenNet offers Roundcube webmail and standard-client access with telephone and email support on weekdays, but no free plan, and its offer is shaped around activists and campaigning groups.

economical.note: The Just Email plan costs 60 pounds a year including VAT for one account with up to four extra aliases.

products.description: A long-standing London ethical internet provider that Ethical Consumer rates top of its email guide, with standard IMAP access and built-in encryption, at a higher yearly price than most privacy mailboxes.

products.name: mail.coop

privacy.note: Ethical Consumer's February 2025 email guide rated mail.coop 50 out of 100 for privacy, 'Reasonably good', and did not list it among providers with end-to-end encryption as standard.

openness.note: mail.coop says it is built on '100% Open Source' software.

portability.note: Both plans include syncing across devices with IMAP and POP3 as well as webmail.

respect.note: mail.coop is cooperatively owned and run by three UK worker cooperatives, and says 'we never sell your data or read your mail', with no advertising or data profiling.

accessibility.note: It offers webmail, standard-client access and telephone support, but no free plan, and mostly serves UK users including former Phone Coop customers.

economical.note: The Basic plan is 24 pounds a year including VAT for one mailbox with 5 GB; Premium is 50 pounds a year for five mailboxes sharing 25 GB.

products.description: The UK's cooperative email provider: ad-free, built on open-source software and cheap at 24 pounds a year, but not end-to-end encrypted and without a free tier.

products.name: Migadu

privacy.note: Migadu's current drawbacks documentation, re-read in October 2026 and last revised in June 2020, says plainly that mail is 'Not encrypted' at rest and recommends users apply end-to-end tools such as GPG themselves; its servers are in France, under a Swiss company.

openness.note: Migadu says it has invested in a new open-source webmail and bases its spam filtering on open-source tools, but the hosted service itself is not published.

portability.note: Migadu's current drawbacks documentation, re-read in October 2026, says it does not offer addresses on its own domains, saying it refuses to lock users in, so mail lives on a domain the user owns and is reached over standard IMAP, POP and SMTP.

respect.note: Migadu's privacy policy, updated December 2024, says it uses no tracking or analytics cookies and collects no behavioural analytics; it is funded by flat-rate subscriptions rather than advertising.

accessibility.note: Migadu's current drawbacks documentation, re-read in October 2026, says it requires a user's own domain name, has an English-only interface and offers no telephone support, which suits people comfortable with DNS more than beginners.

economical.note: The Micro plan costs 19 US dollars a year with unlimited addresses on an account; Mini is 90 dollars a year, and a domain name must be bought separately.

products.description: A Swiss custom-domain mail host that is unusually candid about its limits: cheap, standards-based and free of tracking, but not encrypted at rest and only usable with a domain you own.

products.name: Purelymail

privacy.note: Purelymail's security page says email content is encrypted at rest with the user's password, so even Purelymail cannot read it if password reset is disabled, though search indexes may hold partial content and IMAP decryption happens on its servers; it does not offer end-to-end encryption.

portability.note: Purelymail supports IMAP, POP3 and SMTP with any mail client, unlimited custom domains, and a mail-transfer tool for moving in.

respect.note: Purelymail's privacy policy says selling information or violating privacy are 'NOT part of our business model', and its security page says it will never sell or monetize user data.

accessibility.note: Purelymail's own site lists its weak points: no 24/7 support, occasional blocking by obscure servers, and a UI that 'isn't always the most intuitive'.

economical.note: Simple pricing is 10 US dollars a year with no hard limits on users, domains or storage; heavy users may need pay-per-use advanced pricing.

products.description: A very cheap, no-frills paid mailbox at 10 dollars a year with standard IMAP and password-encrypted storage, run by a small US company with limited support and a less polished interface.
